item.title: Morning Brief — Morning Brief for Friday, May 1, 2026
item.description: DHS funding is signed but the immigration fight shifts to the next spending round, Iran and the Strait of Hormuz keep oil and inflation risk elevated, new video sharpens the White House dinner security fallout, GDP growth and housing strain keep mortgages in focus, Columbus follows the Casey Goodson retrial, Issue 5, the city auditor transition and a Linden police shooting investigation, AI power keeps shifting toward cloud infrastructure, markets close April at records, and Central Ohio turns m
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Friday, May 1st, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top national story this morning is the Homeland Security funding fight, because what looked yesterday like a shutdown and staffing crisis has now turned into a partial political truce. The Associated Press reports President Trump signed a bipartisan bill on April 30 funding the Department of Homeland Security and ending the record shutdown, but without the administration's full immigration-enforcement request attached. That means the immediate operational pressure on TSA pay and basic department functions has eased, but the larger immigration spending battle has not been solved. It has been deferred.

That continuity matters. For the past several days, the question was whether Washington would allow routine security operations to get dragged under by a larger partisan fight. Now the answer is no, at least for the moment. But the administration still wants a much larger enforcement package, and Republican leaders are expected to keep pushing for that through a separate process. So this story has shifted from shutdown risk to round two.

The practical takeaway is that airports and frontline Homeland Security operations may get a little breathing room, but the political incentive to keep escalating on immigration remains fully intact.

The second national story is still the Iran shipping standoff, because the market continues to treat the Strait of Hormuz as unstable enough to keep energy pressure alive. The Associated Press reports Iran's supreme leader on Thursday publicly vowed to protect the country's nuclear and missile capabilities and emphasized Iranian leverage over the strait, even as ceasefire diplomacy remains unresolved. Another AP market report early Friday said Brent crude was still around 111 dollars a barrel. That tells you the market has not priced in a clean normalization story.

The continuity line from earlier this week still holds, but it is getting sharper. This is no longer only a Middle East military story. It is an inflation, rates, and household-cost story for the United States. If traders believe the waterway stays risky, oil stays expensive, inflation fears stay sticky, Treasury yields stay jumpy, and mortgage relief gets harder to sustain. That is why even listeners who do not follow foreign policy closely should keep watching this one.

The important next step is whether any real movement appears on shipping confidence, not just diplomacy headlines. A ceasefire on paper is not enough if insurers, tanker operators, and energy buyers still assume the route can seize up again. Until that confidence returns, oil remains a pressure point that can leak into gas prices, borrowing costs, and consumer mood.

The third national story remains the Supreme Court fight over Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians. The hearing happened on Wednesday, but it is still one of the clearest tests of executive power on the board. The Associated Press reports several conservative justices appeared receptive to the administration's argument that courts should have limited ability to review Homeland Security decisions to end TPS. We will not get a ruling immediately, but the hearing gave the White House a plausible path.

The continuity language here is straightforward. This is still about much more than TPS itself. It is about whether the administration can claim broad freedom to unwind immigration protections quickly and present those moves as mostly insulated from judicial review.

So the watch item is not a same-day outcome. It is whether the administration begins speaking as if it already has a wider lane on immigration, and whether advocates can shift public attention back to the human and procedural costs before the court rules later on.

The fourth national story is the White House Correspondents' Dinner security fallout. Federal prosecutors on Thursday released video showing the moment authorities say Cole Allen charged security at the Washington Hilton while armed and trying to reach President Trump. The new footage, again reported by the Associated Press, matters because this story is moving from a vague security failure into a more documented accountability phase.

The continuity line is that the core question has not changed, but the evidence is getting more concrete. How did a hotel guest in a mixed-use building get close enough to trigger a presidential protection crisis? The video may answer part of the gunfire dispute, but it does not settle the broader confidence problem.

One other national item is worth keeping in frame this morning: the economy is still growing, but not in a way that erases household stress. AP reports first-quarter GDP grew at a 2 percent annual rate, better than late 2025, while consumer spending slowed and residential investment fell again. That mix fits what many households already feel. The top-line economy is not collapsing, but the housing side remains strained and the margin for higher rates is still thin.

That brings us to home lending and mortgages, where the story this morning is that headline relief and daily borrower reality are not exactly the same thing. Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey, released April 30, showed the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.30 percent, up from 6.23 percent a week earlier. Mortgage News Daily's daily index, which had been more sensitive to the recent oil-and-yield volatility, showed a higher 30-year fixed reading of 6.50 percent as of April 29.

That gap is useful. Freddie's survey captures a broader weekly average. Mortgage News Daily reflects day-to-day lender pricing that can swing faster when bond markets get rattled. So the continuity line from yesterday still holds: relief for borrowers is fragile. The late-April dip in rates did not turn into a clean downtrend. Instead, oil risk and Treasury volatility pushed desks back toward repricing.

There was also another signal from Freddie Mac on April 30 that tells you something about the market's posture. In its first-quarter results, Freddie said refinance loans accounted for 42 percent of its single-family volume, the highest quarterly refinance share in four years.

So for listeners thinking about a purchase, refinance, or move this spring, the lesson is not that rates are falling cleanly. It is that windows are opening and closing quickly. If the Iran-driven oil pressure fades and yields calm down, rates could improve again. If not, borrowers may keep living in a market where a seemingly encouraging weekly average does not always match what lenders are quoting in real time.

In Columbus and Central Ohio, the most important ongoing legal story remains the retrial of former Franklin County sheriff's deputy Jason Meade in the 2020 killing of Casey Goodson Jr. NBC4 reported Thursday that testimony resumed with the prosecution continuing to build its case after calling more than a dozen witnesses. The continuity line here is the same one that has mattered all week: this retrial will turn less on broad public emotion than on whether prosecutors can make the use-of-force case feel factually tight and internally consistent for jurors.

Jurors are not being asked to relitigate the public meaning of the case in the abstract. They are being asked whether Meade's use of force was objectively reasonable based on what he believed in the moment. That is why witness sequencing, forensic detail, and contradictions matter so much right now. The case is still in the evidentiary stretch, and that means each day can reshape how clearly the state's theory lands before the defense begins its push.

The second major Columbus story is Issue 5, the May 5 charter amendment that would create a civilian-led crisis response system for some nonviolent emergencies. WOSU reported this week that the proposal would send clinicians, social workers, EMTs, and related responders to selected calls instead of police or fire in situations judged appropriate for that model. The continuity line from the tracker still applies almost perfectly: the debate is no longer mostly about aspiration. It is about implementation.

Supporters have largely won the values argument with voters who like the idea of a different response for behavioral-health and other low-violence incidents. The harder question in the final days is operational. How will dispatch work, what calls qualify, how fast can staffing happen, and how cleanly can the city integrate a new response lane without confusion?

A third Columbus story worth tracking is the city auditor transition. WOSU reports City Council appointed Jacquelin Lewis on April 27 to replace Megan Kilgore, who is leaving in early May. The continuity point this morning is that the selection fight is over, and the credibility phase is beginning. Lewis comes in with public-finance experience and clear City Hall backing. What matters next is what she says first about transparency, fiscal discipline, debt management, and how the city will finance its priorities without weakening public trust.

There is also a new public-safety story in Columbus after a police officer was shot Wednesday night in Linden and the suspect was killed. WOSU reports the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation has taken over the case. Because it happened in North Linden while the Meade retrial continues downtown, the incident is likely to intensify local conversation about officer danger, use of force, and how policing narratives collide in real time. This is a fresh story, so the facts may move quickly over the next several days.

On AI and technology, the most useful update is that the cloud-and-infrastructure realignment is no longer subtle. The Associated Press reported this week that Amazon announced what it called a major expansion of its OpenAI partnership, focused in part on building infrastructure for agent-style systems that can do computer-based work. That came right after Microsoft said it would stop taking a share of OpenAI revenue, even while remaining OpenAI's primary cloud partner.

The continuity line here still holds and is worth repeating because it cuts through the hype. The AI race is not mainly about which chatbot feels smartest in a demo. It is increasingly about who finances compute, who controls cloud distribution, who can support enterprise-grade deployment, and who can absorb the cost of data centers, chips, and power. OpenAI broadening toward Amazon while loosening one part of its Microsoft tie is a sign that the market is reorganizing around infrastructure leverage, not just product novelty.

For businesses, that means AI competition may look more and more like cloud competition.

That leads into the market snapshot. U.S. stocks closed April at records on Thursday. The Associated Press says the S and P 500 rose 73.06 points to 7,209.01, the Dow gained 790.33 to 49,652.14, the Nasdaq added 219.07 to 24,892.31, and the Russell 2000 climbed 60.43 to 2,799.90. Strong earnings, especially from Alphabet, helped investors look past some of the oil volatility and concerns over heavy AI spending.

The market message this morning is not that risk disappeared. It is that earnings strength is still powerful enough to support equities even in an environment where oil is elevated and the inflation story is not fully resolved. That is encouraging, but it also means markets remain sensitive to any sign that energy costs or bond yields are about to break higher again.

For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service says today should be milder than the last couple of days, with a high near 70 and a chance of showers, especially later in the day. Friday night turns cooler, and Saturday looks much chillier, with a high only in the mid-50s and a low in the 30s Friday night. So the practical note is simple: today is the better outdoor window, but do not let the warmer afternoon fool you into putting away the jacket for the weekend.

The through-line this morning is that several big stories have not ended. They have simply changed phase. Homeland Security funding has moved from shutdown drama to the next immigration spending showdown. Iran's shipping pressure has moved from geopolitical headline to daily economic drag. The TPS case has moved from policy argument to a waiting game over executive power. Mortgage relief remains available in flashes, but not yet secure. Columbus is still watching whether the Goodson retrial sharpens into a clearer factual narrative, whether Issue 5 feels operationally credible before Tuesday, and whether the new city auditor defines the role as technical stewardship or broader public reassurance.

So watch these pressure points today: whether energy markets calm at all, whether Washington starts framing the signed DHS bill as closure or only an interim maneuver, whether new details emerge from the White House dinner case, whether mortgage desks move with or against the weekly Freddie Mac signal, whether testimony in the Meade retrial tightens the prosecution's theory, and whether the final messaging around Issue 5 becomes more concrete before Election Day.

That is your Morning Brief for Friday, May 1st. Have a good morning, make the most of the milder stretch before the cooler weekend settles in, and keep an eye on the stories that are still moving from headline into consequence.

Good morning. It is Thursday, April 30th, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top national story this morning is still immigration and executive power, because the Supreme Court has now heard the Trump administration's push to end Temporary Protected Status for migrants from Haiti and Syria. The Associated Press reports that several conservative justices appeared open to the administration's view that these TPS decisions belong largely to the executive branch and may be hard for courts to second-guess. That does not settle the case, and we likely will not get a final ruling until later this summer. But the hearing gave a clearer signal about where the legal pressure point is.

The continuity line from yesterday still holds, but now we can sharpen it. This is not only about immigration policy. It is about whether the administration can turn broad political promises into durable legal authority. The White House wants a wide lane to unwind protections quickly. Opponents want the court to focus on process, fairness, and whether the government followed the law before putting long-settled families back at risk of deportation. So the real watch item is whether the justices treat this as a mostly unreviewable policy choice or as a decision that still has to survive normal legal scrutiny.

That matters well beyond TPS. If the court gives the administration more room here, the ruling could strengthen other efforts to move fast on immigration and claim that judges have only a limited role. If the court pushes back, then the message is that campaign urgency still runs into statutory boundaries. Either way, the hearing has moved the story from abstract rhetoric into a very specific test of presidential reach.

The second national story is the Homeland Security funding fight, because Washington is now dealing with the practical costs of trying to run a core security department without normal appropriations. The Associated Press reports that the House took a step toward a larger package to fund the department and immigration enforcement after White House warnings that emergency money for TSA and other personnel will soon run out. That means this is no longer just another partisan budget brawl tucked inside Capitol Hill procedure. It has become an operational story, with airports, screening, staffing, and public confidence all in the frame.

The important continuity here is that immigration politics and government capacity are colliding. Republicans want to use the budget process to lock in a much larger immigration-enforcement agenda. Democrats are trying to separate basic agency funding from that broader push. The result is that the public gets a very clear view of what happens when symbolic politics starts interfering with routine state function. If this drags further, the biggest visible consequences may show up in travel delays, security staffing strain, and a louder fight over whether the administration is governing or staging leverage plays.

The third national story remains the security fallout from the attempted attack at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner. The Associated Press reported new court-file details on Wednesday saying the suspect allegedly took a hotel-room selfie just before the attack and had prepared for the attempt well in advance. That adds another layer of detail, but the broader story is still about system vulnerability, not biography.

The continuity line is stronger this morning because the questions are getting more precise. How did a hotel guest in a mixed-use venue get close enough to create a presidential protection crisis? What exactly was happening at the outer screening perimeter when the suspect moved? And how much of this was a one-off breakdown versus a structural weakness any future attacker could study? Those are not small questions, because they shape how the Secret Service, event planners, and political institutions think about public events for the rest of this term.

So the watch item today is whether officials provide a tighter operational timeline and whether Thursday's detention hearing produces additional facts. Republicans are already using the episode to revive the push for a White House ballroom, but before that debate really lands, the country still needs a sober accounting of what failed, what held, and what changes now.

For listeners, the point is not to catalogue every federal fight. It is to notice the governing pattern. On immigration, security, and agency funding, the administration is betting that speed and ideological clarity matter more than broad institutional consensus. That raises the stakes of legal fights and implementation failures, because every rushed move becomes a test of law, process, and competence.

Now to the money story, because the same oil pressure we have been tracking is still feeding directly into borrowing costs. Mortgage News Daily said its daily 30-year fixed rate index rose to 6.45 percent on April 29th, up from 6.38 percent a day earlier. Freddie Mac's latest weekly survey, released April 23rd, had the 30-year average at 6.23 percent, but the more immediate daily move is the one that matters this morning because it captures how quickly bond-market nerves returned as oil jumped and Treasury yields rose.

The continuity line from yesterday remains intact. Mortgage relief is still fragile, and it still depends on calmer energy prices and steadier Treasury markets. If traders conclude that higher oil means stickier inflation and fewer Fed cuts, mortgage rates can give back April's improvement very quickly. That is what this week has started to look like.

So the practical takeaway for buyers, refinancers, and anyone watching home affordability is that the rate story is no longer a straight line lower. It is a tug of war. The weekly surveys still show rates below where they were a year ago, but the day-to-day market is reminding borrowers that geopolitical risk and inflation expectations can reverse sentiment fast. If you are shopping this market, the lesson is not panic. It is realism. Affordability is still better than it was at last year's highs, but it is nowhere close to easy.

That brings us back to the energy story itself. The Associated Press reports Brent crude surged nearly 6 percent on Wednesday to settle around 110 dollars and 44 cents a barrel as the Iran shipping confrontation kept traders on edge. The continuity here is simple and important. Markets still do not believe the Strait of Hormuz is safely back to normal. Until there is credible evidence that tanker flow is normalizing and that this is becoming a stable settlement instead of another tactical pause, oil is likely to keep pushing into inflation expectations, consumer costs, and interest-rate assumptions.

In Columbus and Central Ohio, the most urgent civic story is Issue 5, the charter amendment that would create and formalize a community crisis response system for nonviolent emergencies. WOSU reports voters will decide the measure on Tuesday, May 5th, and the coalition behind it has spent years trying to build a response structure centered on clinicians, social workers, EMTs, and other specialized responders rather than default police or fire dispatch in every case.

The continuity line here has shifted from concept to implementation. Yesterday we said the vote was entering its practical phase, and that is even more true now. The broad idea polls as intuitive to many people: not every emergency needs an armed response, and not every person in crisis is best served by a traditional enforcement model. But at the end of campaigns, abstract support is less important than whether voters trust the mechanics. How would dispatch work? How quickly could teams be staffed? How would the city pay for expansion over time? What would happen on the messy calls that do not fit neatly into one category?

The notable thing about this story is that even the Fraternal Order of Police's local leadership moved from suspicion to support after talking with organizers and city officials. That does not eliminate operational questions, but it does tell you this fight is not following the most familiar partisan script. The watch item over the next several days is whether supporters keep translating a humane idea into a credible city system.

The second Columbus story is the retrial of former Franklin County sheriff's deputy Jason Meade in the killing of Casey Goodson Jr. NBC4 reported the prosecution continued building its case on Wednesday as testimony moved deeper into the evidentiary phase. That is the same continuity line we flagged yesterday, and it matters because this is the stage where jurors stop hearing broad narrative claims and start absorbing the details that will shape reasonableness, movement, timing, and credibility.

This retrial has always turned on a specific and difficult legal frame. Jurors are not simply being asked whether Goodson died at Meade's hands. That is undisputed. They are being asked whether Meade's use of force was objectively reasonable based on what he knew at the time. So every witness, every forensic detail, and every dispute over where the gun was or how events unfolded matters enormously. The watch item now is whether prosecutors can make the state's timeline feel more coherent and persuasive than the defense account before the case turns toward the other side's presentation.

The third Columbus story is a quieter one but still important for city governance. WOSU reports Jacquelin Lewis has been chosen as the next Columbus city auditor, replacing Megan Kilgore in early May. The continuity line from yesterday is that the selection itself is settled, but the meaning of the pick is just starting to form. The city auditor's office is not a ceremonial post. It sits at the center of accounting, debt, transparency, and the public's confidence that the city's books match its promises.

So the next five-day watch is not who got the job. It is what Lewis says and does first about rigor, disclosure, and fiscal discipline. Those first signals matter because trust in city finance is usually built quietly and lost loudly.

On AI and technology, the clearest update is that the power structure keeps moving away from a single flagship alliance and toward a harder-edged cloud competition. The Associated Press reports Amazon announced a major expansion of its partnership with OpenAI, focused in part on agent-style systems that can perform computer tasks, just after Microsoft said it would stop taking a share of OpenAI revenue. That is not a small contractual tweak. It is another sign that the AI boom is becoming more distributed, more commercial, and more explicitly tied to cloud leverage.

The continuity line still holds. The AI race is not mainly about chatbots anymore. It is about who owns compute, who can finance massive infrastructure, and who controls enterprise distribution. OpenAI is broadening its cloud relationships. Microsoft is reducing one kind of dependency while protecting another. Amazon is using AWS scale to demand a bigger role in the next phase of AI economics.

For listeners trying to separate hype from durable trend, that is the useful lens. The flashy consumer product will keep changing, but the companies that matter most may be the ones paying for data centers, chips, power, and distribution.

That connects directly to the market snapshot. The Associated Press reports that on Wednesday the S and P 500 slipped less than one tenth of a percent to 7,135.95. The Dow fell 280.12 points, or 0.6 percent, to 48,861.81. The Nasdaq rose just 9.44 points to 24,673.24. The Russell 2000 fell 0.6 percent to 2,739.47. The pattern tells the story. Investors were not in full retreat, but higher oil and higher yields clearly took some oxygen out of the rally.

The market message this morning is that the bull case is still alive, but it is more conditional than it looked earlier in the week. Strong earnings can still support equities, but if energy costs keep rising and the bond market keeps backing away from expected Fed cuts, stocks have to work harder to justify lofty levels.

For Columbus weather, expect a cooler and quieter day after Wednesday's rain. The National Weather Service forecast for Columbus shows Thursday temperatures climbing from the mid-40s in the morning into the upper 50s by late afternoon, with precipitation chances fading to very low levels and a northwest breeze in place. Friday also looks cool, with highs in the upper 50s. So the practical note is simple: you can probably leave the umbrella home today, but keep the jacket.

The through-line this morning is that several big stories are still in the prove-it phase. The administration's immigration agenda now has to persuade the Supreme Court, not just its own supporters. Congress has to show it can fund core security functions without turning every deadline into a stress test. Officials still owe the country a more credible explanation of how the White House dinner security failure happened. Mortgage relief still has to survive oil and yield pressure. Columbus still has to decide whether Issue 5 feels implementable, not just admirable, and the Casey Goodson retrial still has to move from claim to proof in front of jurors.

So watch these pressure points today: any fresh signal from the justices or the administration after the TPS arguments, whether Congress breaks the Homeland Security impasse before operations get shakier, whether the detention hearing in the White House dinner case produces new specifics, whether oil and Treasury yields stay elevated, whether mortgage desks keep repricing upward, whether early-vote messaging around Issue 5 gets more concrete, and whether testimony in the Meade retrial sharpens the factual picture for jurors.

That is your Morning Brief for Thursday, April 30th. Have a good morning, enjoy the cooler and calmer weather in Central Ohio, and keep an eye on the stories that are moving from headline into hard consequence.

Good morning. It is Wednesday, April 29th, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top national story this morning is immigration, because one of the administration's biggest power tests has reached the Supreme Court. The Associated Press reports that the justices are set to hear arguments today over the Trump administration's attempt to end Temporary Protected Status for migrants from Haiti and Syria. That is not just another court hearing on a crowded docket. It is a live test of how far the White House can go in unwinding humanitarian protections that lower courts have said cannot simply be swept aside without following the law.

The continuity line from yesterday still holds, but this morning it is more immediate. Immigration is moving out of the campaign-message phase and into the statutory-limits phase. The administration wants the public to see a broad show of executive control. The courts keep asking a narrower and more consequential question: what does the law actually allow a president and a Homeland Security secretary to do on their own? That is why the TPS hearing matters beyond the specific populations involved. If the court signals a wider tolerance for unilateral executive action, the policy ripple effects could spread well beyond this case.

So the watch item today is not only the outcome, because we will not get that immediately. It is the argument itself. Does the administration persuade the court that the termination decision is largely insulated from review, or do the justices show concern about process, discrimination claims, and the practical disruption that would follow for families who have been living and working here legally for years? The bigger story is executive power, and today's hearing is one of the clearest windows into it.

The second national story remains the Middle East shipping standoff, because the market still does not believe this is safely de-escalating. The Associated Press reports that Iran continues to tie fuller reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to wider concessions, including relief from the U.S. blockade and movement on the war itself. That means we are still stuck in the same uneasy place we flagged yesterday: enough diplomatic motion to prevent a total panic, but nowhere near enough trust to restore normal energy confidence.

That continuity matters because the economic effects are no longer abstract. Oil stayed elevated again as traders priced the possibility that tanker flow could remain constrained or politically contingent. And once oil stays high for more than a headline cycle, it leaks into almost every other part of the economic story. Gasoline gets more expensive. Transportation pressure sticks around longer. Inflation expectations harden. And bond investors get less willing to price an easy path to lower borrowing costs.

The practical takeaway this morning is simple. Until there is credible evidence that shipping lanes are normalizing and that this is becoming a true settlement rather than another temporary bargaining position, energy markets are likely to stay tense. So even listeners who do not follow foreign policy closely should keep watching this story, because it is one of the fastest ways geopolitics can show up in household budgets.

The third national story is the White House Correspondents' Dinner security fallout, where the center of gravity keeps shifting from the suspect to the system. The Associated Press has laid out more detail on how the alleged attacker appears to have gotten inside the Washington Hilton because he was a hotel guest and how the event's outer screening layer was in a transitional moment once the president had already been seated. That does not read like reassurance. It reads like a blueprint for the next round of uncomfortable questions.

The continuity line here is sharper now. This is no longer mainly about the shock of a high-profile attack attempt. It is about whether anyone can give the country a clear operational accounting of how a venue that was part hotel, part political event, and part presidential security zone still produced that vulnerability. Republicans are already using the incident to renew the push for a White House ballroom, but that is downstream from the more basic issue. Before the political argument, there has to be a factual one: where exactly did the perimeter hold, where did it thin out, and what gets changed before the next mixed-use event with the president on site?

So the watch item is whether the official story gets more precise today. If the public gets only broad statements that the system worked, confidence will keep eroding. If investigators can explain timing, access, and procedure in concrete terms, then this story may start to move from spectacle toward actual lesson-learning.

Now to rates, mortgages, and the Fed, where the national and household stories are meeting in one tight knot. Mortgage pricing has edged higher again. Forbes Advisor's April 29 mortgage table puts the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.37 percent, up from 6.27 percent a week earlier, while the 15-year fixed is at 5.53 percent. Those are not catastrophic numbers, but they are still high enough to keep affordability strained and to leave most homeowners with very little refinancing incentive.

The continuity point from yesterday still stands: mortgage relief remains limited and fragile. This morning there is just a cleaner explanation for why. MarketWatch says the 10-year Treasury yield was holding around 4.36 percent ahead of the Fed decision, while oil near 104 dollars a barrel kept the inflation backdrop uncomfortably warm. Add in the political transition around the central bank, with Kevin Warsh moving closer to the chairmanship, and borrowers still do not have a simple path to cheaper money.

So for listeners thinking about home buying, refinancing, or even just whether the housing market will feel easier by summer, the answer this morning is still no clear break yet. If yields stay elevated and energy pressure lingers, mortgage rates can remain stuck in this frustrating middle ground even if the Fed does not move today.

Now to Columbus and Central Ohio, where the biggest continuing courtroom story is still the retrial of former Franklin County deputy Jason Meade in the killing of Casey Goodson Jr. The Associated Press coverage remains the clearest framing: prosecutors say Goodson was shot six times in the back while entering his grandmother's home, while the defense says Meade acted in self-defense because he believed Goodson pointed a gun at him. That core dispute has not changed. What is changing is the stage of the trial.

The continuity language matters here. This is now less about the opening narratives people already know and more about whether the second jury gets a cleaner factual pathway than the first one did before the mistrial. That means witness testimony, forensic detail, and any narrowing of the gun-position dispute matter more than rhetoric. If either side gets a stronger evidentiary foothold over the next couple of days, that will tell us more than the familiar arguments ever could.

This remains one of the most important local trust stories in Columbus. It is about criminal accountability, but it is also about whether the city can get a clearer public resolution to a case that has been hanging over it for years.

The second major local story is the May 5 charter amendment on community crisis response, which is now close enough to Election Day that the politics are giving way to the mechanics. Franklin County's election notice spells out the proposal clearly: create and fund a community crisis response system for calls that need something other than a police-only or fire-only answer, while requiring ongoing oversight and public engagement.

The continuity line from yesterday still fits, but it needs one update. The broad case for the amendment is easy to understand, and many voters likely support the idea in principle. The real question now is whether supporters can keep translating that principle into an operating model people trust. Dispatch rules, staffing, cost, and accountability are no longer side questions. They are the whole late-stage argument. In the next five days, this story will probably be decided less by abstract values than by whether voters feel the implementation case is solid enough.

Another local government story worth tracking is the city auditor transition. WOSU reports that Columbus City Council has now chosen Jacquelin Lewis to replace Megan Kilgore. That means one uncertainty is over, but a more practical one is starting. The office sits at the center of city finances, debt, accounting, and credibility. So the next watch item is not the selection itself. It is what Lewis signals first about transparency, discipline, and how she intends to handle a city that keeps asking residents to trust large and complicated public-spending choices.

For a broader Central Ohio read, Spectrum News says gas prices in Ohio have continued climbing with the Iran situation, with the statewide average for regular at about 4 dollars and 16 cents a gallon and Franklin County around 4 dollars and 15 cents. That matters because it translates the overseas shipping story directly into the local daily-cost story. Columbus listeners do not need to follow every diplomatic twist to feel the result at the pump.

On AI and technology, the most useful update is that the power map keeps becoming more concrete. The Associated Press reports that Amazon announced a major expansion of its partnership with OpenAI just after Microsoft said it would stop taking a share of OpenAI revenue. Put those together and the old story about one dominant alliance keeps giving way to a newer one about multiple cloud giants, enormous infrastructure commitments, and a much more openly commercial AI landscape.

The continuity line still holds, but it is stronger this morning. The AI race is not mainly about model theater anymore. It is about who controls compute, cloud distribution, enterprise access, and financing at scale. OpenAI is broadening its infrastructure base. Microsoft is loosening one revenue tie while keeping strategic positioning. Amazon is trying to convert cloud scale into a deeper seat at the AI table. Republicans are already trying to turn the incident into a new argument for moving more presidential events into a hardened White House ballroom. That may become a political sideshow. How did the perimeter work, where did it fail, and what gets changed before the next high-profile event held in a venue that is part hotel, part press event, and part presidential security zone?

So the watch item is broader than motive alone. Investigators still need to fill in motive, planning, and timeline. If it shifts toward perimeter design, venue access, and coordination between hotel and federal security, then the country may actually learn something useful from what was very close to being much worse.

The second national story remains the Middle East standoff, because the latest diplomatic movement still is not enough to calm energy markets. Reporting over the last day says Iran has floated a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without first settling the broader nuclear dispute, while asking for relief from the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. That sounds, at first glance, like de-escalation. The market reaction says traders do not fully believe it.

That continuity matters. We are still in the same uneasy middle phase where there is just enough diplomacy to prevent a clean panic, but not enough trust to restore normal confidence. Reuters-reported market coverage showed oil climbing again Monday as talks stayed stalled and tanker traffic through Hormuz remained disrupted. Brent settled above 108 dollars a barrel, and U.S. crude also pushed higher. So this morning's practical read is simple: Iran may be signaling flexibility around shipping, but until there is a credible path to a broader settlement, oil traders are going to price the risk as real and ongoing.

Higher oil pushes through the economy unevenly but persistently. It can lift transportation costs, complicate inflation expectations, and make bond markets less willing to assume easy rate relief is coming. In other words, the more stubborn this shipping risk stays, the less comfortable policymakers and households can be.

That takes us straight to immigration and the courts, which remain one of the most active national pressure points this week. The Associated Press reported Friday that the D.C. Circuit blocked Trump's order suspending asylum access at the southern border, saying immigration law still gives people the right to apply for asylum and that the president cannot simply override that structure by proclamation. The asylum ruling did not settle the broader border fight, but it did remind the administration that not every maximal claim of presidential power survives contact with existing law.

So the near-term watch item is whether the Justice Department moves quickly to escalate the asylum case while also using the April 29 TPS hearing to frame a broader message of executive authority. Circuit ruled on April 24 that Trump's order suspending asylum access at the southern border was illegal, saying immigration law gives migrants the right to apply for asylum and that the president cannot just erase that process by proclamation. The through-line this morning is that a lot of major stories are in the verification phase now. Iran is offering a narrower shipping fix, but the deeper deal is still missing. Bankrate's daily table, updated Sunday, April 26, puts the current average 30-year fixed mortgage rate around 6.33 percent, with the national average 30-year fixed APR at 6.40 percent. That is not a bad band relative to the peaks of the last few years, but it is still expensive enough that small shifts matter.

The continuity line from yesterday still holds: this is a workable mortgage market, not a comfortable one. If you are buying or refinancing, the real lever is still the full payment structure, not just the headline rate. Rate locks, credits, points, and seller concessions still matter more than waiting for a perfect drop that may never come. And if oil stays elevated because the Hormuz story does not calm down, it becomes much harder for rates to drift materially lower in the short run.

Here in Columbus and Central Ohio, the Casey Goodson retrial remains one of the most consequential local stories. WOSU reports that opening statements began Thursday, with prosecutors arguing that Jason Meade shot Goodson six times in the back while Goodson was carrying sandwiches into his grandmother's home, and the defense again arguing that Meade believed his life was in danger. The continuity point is that this retrial is now in the evidence phase, and that means the public story starts getting shaped not by summaries of the case but by what witnesses and physical evidence can actually support in court.

This remains bigger than one verdict. The first trial ended in a hung jury. So this second trial is not just another legal proceeding. It is a legitimacy test for the local justice system and for a community that has lived with this case since 2020. Over the next several days, watch whether witness testimony sharpens or softens the central dispute over Goodson's gun, what Meade could see, and whether jurors are given a cleaner factual path than they were the first time.

Another Columbus continuity story is the city auditor vacancy. The City of Columbus says Council is taking applications for the role created by Megan Kilgore's resignation, and the official vacancy page makes clear that the appointee will serve until January 1, 2028. The city also emphasizes the scale of the job: more than one hundred full-time employees in the office, roughly a 20 million dollar operating budget, and a central role in the city's accounting, debt, tax, reporting, and financial systems.

That is why this is not just an inside-government personnel story. It is a competence story. Columbus is large enough and financially complex enough that this office touches nearly every serious budget, bond, and tax question the city has. So the test over the next week is whether Council treats the appointment as a real search for financial credibility or as something softer and more political. The public materials now put the stakes in writing. The next thing to watch is whether applicant names, interview plans, or decision timing start to surface.

The May 5 charter amendment on emergency response is also moving into its final stretch. This is the proposal that would create a city-run twenty-four-seven non-police crisis response option for certain mental-health, substance-use, homelessness, and wellness-related calls routed through 911. The broad concept is easy to explain. The hard part is still implementation. Cost, staffing, dispatch rules, and responder safety are the details that will determine whether voters see this as a practical redesign or as an underbuilt mandate.

The Columbus NWSL and McCoy Park story also stays active. WOSU has already reported that Columbus secured the 2028 NWSL expansion team and that the city agreement requires a working group and a replacement-park plan on a fast timeline. Franklin County then added another layer this week, approving a framework that includes up to 25 million dollars over 15 years and says the ownership group must produce 12 million dollars in community benefits. The continuity line here is unchanged: the franchise is the easy headline, but the public-trust test is still the neighborhood follow-through.

That means the next few days are not really about celebration. They are about whether the public can see the first signs of a credible replacement process for McCoy Park and whether city and county leaders can show that the community-benefit language has real teeth. If those details stay vague, skepticism will stay high. If officials start naming participants, dates, and deliverables, the politics of the deal may soften.

On AI and technology, the most useful frame this morning is that the money keeps getting bigger because compute has become the real battleground. TechCrunch reports that Google plans to invest up to 40 billion dollars in Anthropic, with 10 billion committed now and more tied to performance targets and infrastructure needs. That follows another large Anthropic-Amazon compute arrangement and reinforces the same basic point we have been making: the AI race is no longer just about model demos or consumer mindshare. It is about capital, chips, cloud contracts, and power.

That matters to regular listeners for two reasons. First, it helps explain why tech investors are still rewarding infrastructure-adjacent companies so aggressively. Second, it is a reminder that the economic footprint of AI is increasingly physical. This is data centers, electricity load, chip supply, and financing scale, not just software hype. If the spending keeps concentrating around the firms that control compute, then the winners of the next phase may be the suppliers and platforms as much as the model makers themselves.

That connection showed up again in Friday's markets. AP reports that the S and P 500 rose 0.8 percent to 7,165.08 and set another all-time high, while the Nasdaq climbed 1.6 percent to 24,836.60. The Dow slipped 0.2 percent to 49,230.71. Intel surged 23.6 percent for its best day since 1987 after a strong earnings report, which is a useful snapshot of how strongly investors are still responding to companies that can plausibly claim an AI hardware or infrastructure angle.

So the market message heading into Sunday is mixed but still constructive. Equities are willing to look through a lot right now, including geopolitical stress, as long as earnings and AI spending stay strong enough. But the risk is still obvious. If Iran-related energy disruption worsens, or if rate expectations harden, the same market that is celebrating infrastructure demand could turn quickly toward inflation anxiety and multiple compression.

For Columbus weather, the latest National Weather Service forecast says the city starts Sunday cloudy, then gradually clears with a high near 72. Sunday night turns mostly clear with a low around 50. Monday looks warmer and mostly sunny with a high near 81 before showers and thunderstorms return late Monday night into Tuesday. So the practical read is that today is the recovery day. The gray start should give way to a solid afternoon, and the next better chance for disruption does not arrive until late tomorrow.

The through-line this morning is that several of the biggest stories are no longer in the announcement stage. They are in the proof stage. Washington can say the security response worked, but now the public will want to know how an armed suspect got as close as he did. Trump can say Iran only needs to call, but what matters is whether a real channel survives. The administration can appeal the asylum ruling, but the legal theory now has a serious test attached to it. Warsh can promise Fed independence, but borrowers and markets will judge that by what actually happens to rates. Columbus can talk about accountability, replacement parks, and crisis-response reform, but the next few days will show whether those promises are getting operational.

So watch nine things today and this week: the motive and security review after the Washington shooting, whether any Iran back channel revives in Pakistan or Oman, how fast the asylum case is pushed up the ladder, whether Warsh's path tightens the focus on mortgage rates, what testimony reveals in the Goodson retrial, whether the auditor search becomes more public, how specific the emergency-response campaign gets before May 5, whether the NWSL replacement-park process shows early structure, and whether AI infrastructure euphoria can keep outrunning geopolitical risk in the market.

That is your Morning Brief for Sunday, April 26th. Have a good morning, take the clearer afternoon if you can get it, and keep an eye on the stories that now have to prove more than they can promise.

item.title: Morning Brief — Morning Brief for Saturday, April 25, 2026
item.description: Iran ceasefire talks move to Pakistan, a federal court blocks Trump’s asylum ban, Fed leadership pressure keeps mortgage watchers on edge, Columbus housing and government stories stay active, AI spending keeps accelerating, markets close the week at records, and Columbus dries out after overnight rain.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Saturday, April 25th, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top story this morning is the Iran ceasefire track, because the diplomatic lane is still open, but it is open in the most fragile way possible. The Associated Press reports that President Trump is sending Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Pakistan for another round of talks tied to Iran’s foreign minister. Iran is still rejecting direct negotiations with U.S. officials, so Pakistan is acting as the intermediary again. That matters because this is not a clean peace process. It is a high-stakes effort to keep a tense pause from snapping while the economic fallout keeps spreading through shipping and energy markets.

The continuity line from earlier in the week still holds. The shooting may have slowed, but the Strait of Hormuz is still not functioning normally enough for markets to relax. AP reports that the ceasefire remains in place, but disrupted traffic through Hormuz is still clouding the global outlook. Iran has partly reopened its airspace and resumed some flights, which suggests some stabilization. At the same time, Washington announced new sanctions on a Chinese refinery and on shipping companies involved in moving Iranian oil, which means pressure is still being applied even while negotiators try to keep talks alive.

So this morning’s real question is not whether officials can produce another headline about diplomacy. It is whether they can reduce the practical risk premium now embedded in oil, shipping, inflation expectations, and consumer psychology. If the Pakistan channel produces even a modest framework, markets may decide the worst-case energy scenario is less likely. If the talks sputter, oil can move right back to the center of every conversation about inflation, interest rates, and household costs. For now, the watch is simple: whether indirect talks become a durable negotiating structure, whether the Strait becomes more usable, and whether the ceasefire starts to look like an actual transition rather than a nervous timeout.

The second national story is immigration and executive power. A federal appeals court on Friday blocked Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border. AP reports that the D.C. Circuit found immigration law gives people the right to apply for asylum at the border and that the president cannot override that process unilaterally. The administration is expected to seek further review, so this is not the end of the fight, but it is a significant legal setback for one of the administration’s core border policies.

Why this matters beyond the immediate policy dispute is that it is another reminder that several of the administration’s biggest moves are now running into harder judicial boundaries. The ruling does not instantly transform conditions at the border, because other legal and logistical constraints remain in place. But it does reassert that Congress wrote a process and presidents do not simply get to replace it with their own. Over the next few days, watch whether the Justice Department moves quickly toward the full appeals court or the Supreme Court, and watch whether the White House treats this as a legal appeal story or a broader political mobilization story.

The third national and economic story is the Federal Reserve pressure campaign, because it still touches mortgages, markets, and consumer borrowing more directly than a lot of people realize. AP reports that the Justice Department has ended its criminal investigation into Fed chair Jerome Powell over the central bank’s renovation project. The immediate consequence is that Kevin Warsh, Trump’s nominee to replace Powell when Powell’s chair term ends on May 15, now has a clearer path in the Senate.

The important part for listeners is not the Washington drama by itself. It is the rate backdrop. AP notes that Powell and other Fed officials have been reluctant to cut rates quickly while they assess the inflation effects of the Iran war and higher energy costs. That is exactly why this story belongs in the same conversation as mortgage rates. If oil stays elevated and the market believes the next Fed chair could be more politically responsive, borrowing costs can stay jumpy even when headline mortgage averages improve.

On home lending, the rate picture this morning is steady but not loose. Freddie Mac’s weekly survey for April 23 showed the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.23 percent and the 15-year fixed at 5.58 percent. Bankrate’s Saturday tables are a little higher on a lender-survey basis, with the current average 30-year fixed interest rate at 6.33 percent and the national average 30-year fixed APR at 6.40 percent. That spread is useful. It tells you the market is not in free fall and not in panic either. It is hovering in a still-expensive range where small moves in oil, Treasuries, or Fed expectations can change the math quickly.

So the borrower guidance remains practical and unglamorous. If you are buying, focus on the real payment, the APR, the points, and the lock terms instead of waiting for an obvious all-clear signal. There is no all-clear signal right now. There is a narrow workable band. In Central Ohio, that means the difference between a manageable purchase and a strained one is still likely to come from the house price, the down payment, and the lender credits more than from a dramatic rate drop between this weekend and next week.

Here in Columbus, the freshest city-government story is housing stability. Mayor Andrew Ginther’s office this week announced nearly 3 million dollars in housing stability investments for eviction prevention, legal assistance, and housing stabilization services. The city says the money will move through its new Division of Housing Stability and then advance to City Council. That makes this more than a press release. It is a test of whether Columbus can shift a little more of its housing response upstream, before people fall all the way into eviction or homelessness.

This matters because the local housing conversation has been split for a while between big-picture supply questions and emergency shelter pressure. This proposal sits in the middle. It is about the people who are still housed but vulnerable, the residents who may need legal help, dispute resolution, or short-term stabilization before a problem becomes a crisis. The story to watch next is whether Council moves the package quickly, and whether city leaders can show that prevention spending is measurable enough to survive scrutiny in a budget environment where almost every dollar is contested.

The Casey Goodson retrial is also still one of the most consequential stories in Central Ohio. WOSU reports that opening statements began on April 23, with prosecutors arguing that former deputy Jason Meade shot Goodson six times in the back while Goodson carried a bag of sandwiches into his grandmother’s home. The defense is again framing the case around Meade’s claim that he believed his life was in danger. That means the retrial is now fully in its public narrative phase, where the basic theory of the case is no longer abstract.

The reason to keep this in the brief is that the case is not just about one courtroom. It remains a civic legitimacy test for Columbus and Franklin County. The first trial ended in a hung jury. The second trial now has to answer the same deep questions under even sharper scrutiny: what Meade saw, whether Goodson posed a threat, how much weight jurors give to competing accounts, and whether a community that has waited more than five years can accept the process even if it cannot agree with the outcome. Over the next several days, watch how witness testimony either strengthens or weakens the central dispute over whether Goodson was raising his gun or whether it remained holstered until after the shooting.

Another continuity story to watch is the Columbus city auditor vacancy. The city’s vacancy page makes clear that whoever Council appoints will serve until January 1, 2028, finishing the first two years of Megan Kilgore’s term after her May 4 resignation. That still sounds procedural, but it is a serious operational decision. The office runs a large finance and tax apparatus, and this is not the kind of seat the city can afford to fill casually.

What matters now is whether Council treats the selection like a real finance search instead of a low-visibility political appointment. The job pays enough, controls enough, and sits close enough to every major budget and tax question that the standard should be obvious: municipal finance competence first, campaign or personal relationships far behind it. If applicant materials or interview plans start to surface in the coming days, that story will get more concrete quickly.

The May 5 charter amendment on emergency response is also nearing decision time. The proposal would create a 24-7 non-police crisis response option integrated with 911 for certain behavioral health, homelessness, and wellness-related calls. The policy case remains compelling because not every emergency needs the same responder. But now that voting is approaching, the arguments are going to get more specific. Cost, staffing, dispatch rules, and safety thresholds are the parts that will matter most in the final stretch.

The NWSL and McCoy Park story also remains in the accountability phase, not the celebration phase. Columbus officially has the league’s 18th franchise for 2028, but WOSU’s reporting still matters here because the city agreement came with a 15-day deadline to form a working group for replacement park planning and a 60-day deadline to produce a plan. The broader point is unchanged from earlier this week: Columbus succeeded in landing the team, but now has to prove the public-private deal can produce real replacement value for the neighborhood that lost McCoy Park.

On AI and technology, the most useful signal in the last 24 hours is how much the race is turning into a compute and capital story. TechCrunch reports that Google plans to invest up to 40 billion dollars in Anthropic, with 10 billion committed now and more tied to performance targets and infrastructure needs. Strip away the branding, and the takeaway is straightforward. The next phase of AI is not just about who has the smartest model. It is about who can secure chips, data-center capacity, cloud relationships, and enough money to keep scaling.

That story connected directly to markets on Friday. AP reports that Intel had its best day since 1987 after a strong profit report, with CEO Lip-Bu Tan saying the next wave of AI is lifting demand for the company’s chips and products. So the AI trade is becoming clearer. Investors are rewarding companies that can plausibly claim they are selling the picks and shovels, not just the dream. The pressure point is whether that spending can eventually produce durable margins instead of just bigger capex plans and louder promises.

Now the market snapshot. Wall Street closed the week with more records on Friday. AP reports that the S&P 500 rose 0.8 percent to 7,165.08, the Nasdaq gained 1.6 percent to 24,836.60, and the Dow slipped 0.2 percent to 49,230.71. The headline drivers were Intel’s surge, continuing earnings strength, and some hope that the Iran situation may not spin into its worst economic scenario. But the market message is still mixed rather than cleanly bullish.

Oil is the reason. Brent crude for June settled at 105 dollars and 33 cents a barrel on Friday, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.30 percent. That combination tells you the market is still trying to price two different futures at once. One future says earnings and AI demand can keep carrying equities higher. The other says one bad Hormuz headline can quickly reprice inflation, transport costs, and rate expectations. Going into the weekend, the market is choosing optimism, but it is doing so with a hand still on the brake.

For Columbus weather, the overnight rain should give way to a better day. The National Weather Service forecast for Columbus says there is a chance of showers mainly before 9 a.m., then mostly cloudy skies with a high near 70. Saturday night drops to around 46, and Sunday looks better with mostly sunny skies and another high near 70. So the practical read is simple: the first part of the day may still feel damp and unsettled, but the washout risk fades pretty quickly.

The through-line this morning is that several important stories are shifting from announcement to verification. Iran has another diplomatic opening, but it still needs proof. The asylum ruling is a legal brake, but it still has to survive the next appeal. Mortgage rates are lower than they were earlier this month, but they are still tied to oil, Fed politics, and bond-market nerves. Columbus is putting new money into housing stability, but the real test is whether prevention dollars can move fast enough to matter. The Goodson retrial has started, but now the evidence has to carry the weight of years of public distrust. And the NWSL deal is done, but the city still has to make good on the neighborhood promises attached to it.

So watch eight things this weekend: whether Pakistan-hosted Iran talks produce a framework instead of another pause, whether oil finally eases, whether the White House races the asylum ruling back toward the Supreme Court, whether Warsh’s path to the Fed chair tightens the focus on rate cuts, whether Columbus advances the housing stability package, how testimony lands in the Goodson retrial, what Council reveals about the auditor search, and whether the first concrete McCoy Park replacement steps actually appear on schedule.

That is your Morning Brief for Saturday, April 25th. Have a good morning, enjoy the drier second half of the day, and keep an eye on the stories that now need to prove themselves.

item.description: Iran blockade diplomacy and Pentagon turnover, the Shreveport gun investigation, mortgage-rate crosscurrents, Columbus' NWSL and McCoy Park follow-through, the city auditor search, the Casey Goodson retrial, AI spending at Tesla, market records and oil risk, and a mild Columbus forecast.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Thursday, April 23rd, and this is your Morning Brief.

The top story this morning is the U.S.-Iran standoff, because the ceasefire extension has not yet produced the one thing markets, diplomats, and oil buyers actually need: a workable path back to negotiations. Al Jazeera reports that Iranian officials say they want dialogue, but are blaming the U.S. naval blockade and what they call broken commitments for the stall. The White House says President Trump has not set a firm deadline for an Iranian proposal. That makes the current posture less like a settled ceasefire and more like a pause under pressure.

The pressure is visible at sea. Reporting overnight says Iran's Revolutionary Guard captured two foreign vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and opened fire on a third, while U.S. Central Command says the American blockade has turned back dozens of vessels linked to Iranian ports. So the continuity line from yesterday is sharper today. The ceasefire did not expire, but the operating environment around Hormuz is still tense enough to move oil, shipping, and inflation expectations.

There is also a major Pentagon turnover story wrapped into the same moment. The Associated Press reports that Navy Secretary John Phelan is leaving effective immediately, the first military service secretary to depart in Trump's second term. Navy Undersecretary Hung Cao is now acting secretary. No official reason was given, but the timing is hard to ignore: the Navy is enforcing a blockade around Iran, the administration is pushing shipbuilding changes, and Pentagon leadership has already seen a string of high-level removals.

The practical watch list is direct. Watch whether Iran actually sends a negotiating team. Watch whether Pakistan or another mediator can keep the diplomatic lane open. Watch whether the Strait of Hormuz produces another vessel seizure or warning shot. And watch Brent crude. Bloomberg had Brent around 102 dollars a barrel early Thursday, and once oil is back above 100, this stops being a foreign-policy story only. It becomes a household-cost story.

The second national story is the Shreveport mass shooting investigation. AP reports that federal court records say the gun used to kill eight children in Louisiana was believed to have been stolen from a truck weeks before the attack. Charles Ford, the man who previously had the weapon, has been charged with being a felon in possession of a firearm and making false statements to federal agents.

This remains, first, a domestic violence story. Eight children are dead, two women were wounded, and the alleged gunman, Shamar Elkins, died after a police chase. But the investigative focus is widening as authorities reconstruct how the firearm moved before the attack.

The question for the next several days is not only whether Ford is prosecuted. It is whether investigators identify any missed opportunity before the shooting: a prior warning sign, a report that should have been made, a point where a firearm restriction should have mattered more than it did. Those details will shape whether this case becomes a broader accountability story about domestic violence risk, gun access, and enforcement gaps.

Now to home lending and mortgage rates. The rate picture is better than it was a few weeks ago, but it is not simple. Freddie Mac's latest weekly survey, current as of April 16th, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.30 percent and the 15-year fixed at 5.65 percent, a four-week low. Bankrate's Thursday morning purchase-rate table was similar at the headline level, with the average 30-year fixed around 6.32 percent and the 15-year fixed around 5.68 percent.

Fortune, using Optimal Blue lock data reviewed April 22nd, had the average 30-year conforming rate at 6.231 percent and the 15-year at 5.524 percent. The message is useful: rates are drifting, not collapsing.

For borrowers, the reason is familiar. Mortgage pricing is still taking cues from the 10-year Treasury, oil, inflation expectations, and confidence in the Fed. If Brent stays over 100 dollars because Hormuz remains unstable, bond traders are going to keep asking whether energy costs feed back into inflation. If politics around the Federal Reserve keeps looking noisy, that can also show up in term premiums and lender caution.

So the practical guidance is unchanged. Do not shop from a headline average. Shop from the payment, the APR, the points, the lock period, and the lender credits. If you are buying in Central Ohio, run the numbers a quarter point higher than your first quote. The borrowers who make the cleanest decisions right now are the ones treating 6-ish percent financing as a planning environment, not a temporary inconvenience that will obviously vanish before closing.

Here in Columbus, the NWSL story has moved from celebration into follow-through. The league has officially awarded Columbus its 18th franchise, set to begin play in 2028, after Columbus City Council and Franklin County approved public support for the project. Axios Columbus reports the team will be backed by Haslam Sports Group, Nationwide, and Drs. Christine and Pete Edwards, and that the club will have its own resources for ticketing, marketing, and operations even while using some Crew infrastructure.

But the McCoy Park issue is still the local trust test. WOSU reported earlier this week that City Council approved the city's 25 million dollar agreement in a split vote, with amendments meant to address replacement park planning. That means the political question is no longer whether Columbus can land the team. It can. The question is whether city leaders and the ownership group can make the public believe the neighborhood did not lose a promised community asset in a rushed deal.

The next markers are concrete. Columbus Recreation and Parks has a short deadline to form a working group and a 60-day timeline for a replacement park plan. Residents will be looking for more than warm language. They will be looking for site details, money details, construction dates, public access commitments, and proof that the process is not simply a post-vote cleanup exercise.

Another local government story worth keeping active is the city auditor vacancy. Megan Kilgore is set to leave May 4 for a private-sector role tied to the municipal bond market, and City Council has opened the appointment process. The city's own vacancy page makes clear why this is more than a ceremonial post: the auditor is the city's chief accounting officer, the job pays 248,345 dollars in 2026, and the office manages more than 100 full-time positions and a 20 million dollar annual budget.

The appointee will serve until January 1st, 2028, unless voters later choose someone else to complete the term. The auditor's office touches income tax collection, payroll, debt, investments, revenue estimates, financial reporting, and the systems that keep city government running.

So watch for names, qualifications, and transparency. Columbus does not need a placeholder with a friendly biography. It needs someone who can step into a complicated finance shop immediately, protect the city's credit credibility, and explain public money clearly at a time when local spending decisions are already under scrutiny.

The Casey Goodson retrial remains active too. Jury selection is underway for former Franklin County deputy Jason Meade, who is charged with murder and reckless homicide in the 2020 shooting death of Casey Goodson Jr. The first trial ended in a hung jury in 2024. Axios Columbus notes that the defense is expected to argue self-defense, which would require prosecutors to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the shooting was not justified.

This is one of those stories where a quiet procedural day still matters. Jury selection, early rulings, and the first framing of the evidence will shape how the trial is received. Columbus has already lived through years of disagreement over this case: whether Goodson posed a threat, what Meade saw, what the lack of body camera footage leaves unresolved, and whether the justice system can produce an answer that the first jury could not.

The story to watch over the next few days is pace and posture. Does jury selection stay on track? Do opening arguments begin cleanly? Do prosecutors and defense lawyers preview a meaningfully different case than the first trial? The retrial is not just a courtroom event. It is a civic stress test that many residents have been waiting on for more than five years.

The May 5th community crisis response amendment also stays on the local radar. The Columbus Safety Collective says the ballot measure would create a non-police crisis response system integrated with 911 for calls involving behavioral health, wellness checks, homelessness, and similar situations. Axios reports the proposal would move Columbus toward a 24-7 alternative response program, with broader buildout over the next several years.

The policy argument is easy to understand: not every call needs the same response. The implementation questions are harder. Dispatch has to know when to send whom. Clinicians, social workers, peer supporters, EMTs, and police have to understand handoffs and safety rules. Voters now have less than two weeks before the election, so the next movement will likely come through endorsements, opposition messaging, or practical questions about cost and staffing.

On AI and technology, the most useful story this morning is Tesla's earnings report, because it captures the broader shift in the tech market. Reuters reports that Tesla lifted its 2026 spending plan to more than 25 billion dollars as Elon Musk pours money into artificial intelligence, robotics, chips, robotaxis, and manufacturing capacity. Tesla reported positive free cash flow and adjusted earnings that beat expectations, but revenue missed estimates and investors pushed the stock lower after Musk described a major increase in capital spending.

That tension is the AI story in miniature. Investors still want exposure to the next computing cycle, but they are also asking how much cash has to be burned before the promised revenue shows up. Tesla is not pitching itself as only an electric vehicle company anymore. It is asking the market to value self-driving software, humanoid robots, in-house chips, AI training infrastructure, and future autonomous fleets.

The question is whether the core business can support that ambition while the new businesses mature. Across the sector, companies are learning that the market will reward an AI story, but it will increasingly demand evidence: customers, margins, power access, chip supply, and a credible timeline to revenue.

Now the market snapshot. AP reports that U.S. stocks set more records Wednesday. The S&P 500 rose 1 percent to 7,137.90, the Dow added about 341 points to 49,490.03, and the Nasdaq climbed 1.6 percent to 24,657.57. Strong earnings helped, with GE Vernova and other companies giving investors a reason to look past some geopolitical risk.

But the market is not floating above the news. Bloomberg reported early Thursday that the rally was pausing as oil climbed and Iran talks remained in limbo. S&P 500 futures were lower, and Brent was around 102 dollars and 60 cents a barrel. The 10-year Treasury was recently around 4.3 percent in market reporting, which is still high enough to matter for mortgages, growth stocks, and rate-sensitive parts of the economy.

So the tone is split. The equity market is acting like earnings are good enough to keep risk appetite alive. The oil market is acting like the Hormuz story is not solved. The bond market is not giving borrowers a clean green light. That means today could be another headline-sensitive session, especially if there is a fresh update from the Strait of Hormuz, the White House, Iran, or major earnings after the bell.

For Columbus weather, plan on a mild spring day with more clouds than drama. Public forecast aggregators for Columbus show highs roughly in the low 70s, a nighttime low around the low 50s, light wind, and a modest chance of rain. Today is the more usable day, while late Friday into the weekend carries the better rain and storm signal.

The practical version is simple. It should be comfortable for errands, school pickup, lunch outside, or a walk after work. Keep a light layer around for the morning and evening, and keep an eye on Friday if your plans are outdoors.

The through-line today is consequence. The Iran ceasefire was extended, but Hormuz is still unstable. Mortgage rates improved, but oil and Treasury yields still have veto power. Columbus won an NWSL franchise, but now has to prove the McCoy Park promises are real. The city auditor search is open, but the seriousness of the process will be judged by the people who apply and the way Council handles them. The Casey Goodson retrial is underway, but the first meaningful signals will come from jury selection and early courtroom framing. And in tech, Tesla's AI spending shows how expensive the next phase of the race is becoming.

So watch seven things today: oil above 100, any new vessel incident near Hormuz, market reaction to Tesla's spending plan, McCoy Park replacement details, auditor applicant names, the pace of jury selection in the Goodson retrial, and sharper arguments around the crisis response ballot issue.

That is your Morning Brief for Thursday, April 23rd. Have a good morning, keep the umbrella optional today but closer tomorrow, and watch the stories that have moved from announcement into accountability.
